segments.t: In the hallway at ASK, Hervé teases Camille following the explosive revelation about her parentage. Camille struggles with how her colleagues perceive her, while Hervé tries to cheer her up with movie references. Let's listen to the scene in French first.
Arrête, Jean Gabin, c'est Camille!
Ne lui en veux pas trop.
Il te transfère sa haine pour Mathias.
C'est horrible, je suis devenue une autre.
Personne à l'agence ne me reconnaît.
C'est comme dans le film La Moustache.
Le type se rase, personne ne remarque.
Non, c'est exactement le contraire.
Tout le monde pense que j'ai changé.
Que Mathias soit mon père ne change rien.
C'est plutôt comme dans Blade Runner.
Quand on découvre que c'est un réplicant.
On t'aime quand même, Camillette!
Let's examine how Hervé and Camille discuss her new status step by step to understand the humor and emotion.
Arrête, Jean Gabin, c'est Camille!
'Stop it, Jean Gabin, it's Camille!' Herve calls out 'stop!' in the casual 'you' command, teasing a scowling coworker via the surname of cinema's classic tough guy.
Ne lui en veux pas trop.
'Do not hold it against him too much.' That whole line turns on a classic French idiom: literally 'wanting of it to someone' means holding a grudge against them.
Il te transfère sa haine pour Mathias.
'He transfers his hatred for Mathias to you.' Notice how 'his' before 'hatred' matches the thing owned rather than the male speaker — unlike English, where 'his' tracks the owner.
C'est horrible, je suis devenue une autre.
'It is horrible, I have become someone else.' Word for word, Camille says 'I am become an other' — 'become' pairs with 'am' rather than 'have' in the past.
Personne à l'agence ne me reconnaît.
'Nobody at the agency recognizes me.' Here 'recognize' is built from 're-' plus 'to know' — literally 'knowing someone again' when you see them.
C'est comme dans le film La Moustache.
'It is like in the movie The Mustache.' One versatile connector covers both 'like' and 'as' in French, while the title word is the exact source of English 'mustache'.
Le type se rase, personne ne remarque.
'The guy shaves, nobody notices.' Calling a man 'the type' is breezy everyday French for 'the guy', and 'shaves' literally says 'shaves himself'.
Non, c'est exactement le contraire.
'No, it is exactly the opposite.' Where English says 'the opposite', French reaches for a cognate of 'contrary' — a handy chunk whenever you want to flip someone's point around.
Tout le monde pense que j'ai changé.
'Everyone thinks that I have changed.' Literally 'all the world thinks': French expresses 'everyone' through 'all the world' and treats it as a single unit.
Que Mathias soit mon père ne change rien.
'Mathias being my father changes nothing.' Opening with 'that Mathias be my father' packages the whole fact as the subject, while 'not ... nothing' wraps around 'changes'.
C'est plutôt comme dans Blade Runner.
'It is rather like in Blade Runner.' That word meaning 'rather' comes from 'more' fused with 'soon' — much like English saying 'I would sooner compare it to this'.
Quand on découvre que c'est un réplicant.
'When you find out that he is a replicant.' French uses impersonal 'one' where English uses general 'you' for a viewer watching a movie, and 'find out' literally means 'uncover'.
On t'aime quand même, Camillette!

'We love you anyway, Camillette!' Literally 'when same', that two-word expression is how you'll hear French speakers say 'all the same' or 'anyway', topped off by an affectionate '-ette' nickname. Now let's listen to the whole dialogue again.

Ne lui en veux pas trop.

C'est horrible, je suis devenue une autre.

Non, c'est exactement le contraire.

Que Mathias soit mon père ne change rien.
C'est plutôt comme dans Blade Runner.
